conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve been having a lot of diarrhea—up to eight times today—and I can’t keep anything down, not even my tube feeds. My blood sugar was really high too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, started yesterday. I also feel this weird 'electricity' all over my body for the past few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We’ll check your electrolytes. Did you eat anything different recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had seafood in ___ a few days ago. I think that might have triggered this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll test your stool to rule out infections. Your blood sugar was 497 in the ER, so we’ve already given you insulin and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. My abdominal pain is about the same as usual, not worse. But I just can’t tolerate food or feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on bowel rest for now and give IV fluids. We’ll start tube feeds slowly once your nausea improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my 'electric' feeling—is that from high sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. It could be neuropathy from your diabetes. We’ll monitor it and adjust your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool tests came back negative for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not a bacterial one. Given your history of chronic pancreatitis and gastroparesis, this may be a flare-up related to your pancreas condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I ate seafood—could that still be a factor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might have irritated your system, but it doesn’t look like a foodborne infection. We’ll focus on managing your underlying conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting your tube feeds at 5 cc/hr. We’ll increase slowly if you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous—I usually get pain when I start feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. If you have pain, we’ll pause and reassess. You’ll have IV pain meds available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had some setbacks with the feeds due to pain, so we had a team meeting to discuss next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What did you decide?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think your GJ tube might be clogged or not placed optimally. We’re scheduling a tube revision with interventional radiology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a procedure where they replace the tube using imaging guidance. It’s not open surgery, and you’ll be awake but sedated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do it if it might help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tube revision was successful. The new tube is in the right place in your jejunum. We’ll wait a few hours and restart feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I hope this one works better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re tolerating the new tube well. Feeds are at 20 cc/hr with no pain so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I actually feel a bit better. My 'electric' feeling is less intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your blood sugar is also more stable—around 200. We’ve increased your long-acting insulin to 34 units nightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I was on 90 units at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Since you weren’t eating, we lowered it to 30 units. Now that you’re feeding again, we’re increasing it gradually to avoid lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a fall yesterday on your way to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I slipped. My wrist hurts, and my shoulder feels weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: X-rays show no fractures in your wrist or shoulder. Ortho thinks it’s a wrist sprain and possible rotator cuff issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no break?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. We’ve put your wrist in a splint and recommend a sling. Your PCP will order an MRI later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your magnesium is low, which might contribute to the 'electric' sensation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can we fix that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re giving you supplements. It should help with the nerve symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture showed mixed flora—likely contamination. No infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had some vaginal discharge for months. Should I get checked?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but you declined the exam. Please follow up with your PCP after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge soon. Your nutrition is stable—you’ve actually gained weight despite not eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize that. I feel like I haven’t eaten in weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: But your albumin is normal, so you’re getting enough through the tube. We’re weaning your IV pain meds and switching to oral Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay with that. I don’t want to stay on IV meds forever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added some new meds for constipation—senna, docusate, and bisacodyl. Your narcotics cause this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had some bright red blood—was that from hemorrhoids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. Your hemoglobin is stable, so no concern now. Keep up the bowel regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sleep? I’ve been struggling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding trazodone and adjusting Ambien. Also reducing zolpidem dose to avoid side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re finalizing your discharge plan for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What do I need to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue tube feeds as tolerated. Take your new insulin dose—34 units at night. Use Dilaudid for pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bowel meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all of them—lactulose, senna, docusate, bisacodyl. They’ll help prevent constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my PCP for the MRI and vaginal check?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And call if your blood sugar goes too high or low, or if you can’t tolerate feeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’re alert, walking independently, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep up with your follow-ups and medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in the clinic if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my asthma. I’ve been using my inhalers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue Advair and albuterol as prescribed. No changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I almost forgot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Discharge papers are ready. Nurse will go over them with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll review them carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let us know if you have any questions after you get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll follow up with your PCP to coordinate care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We want to make sure you stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will assist you with discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.
